topics.title: Brunei Citizenship Requirements
topics.summary: Ordinary naturalisation in Brunei has a long residence baseline, Malay-language assessment and a discretionary grant. Registration for other cohorts and possession of permanent residence are not themselves naturalisation.
topics.scope: Selected ordinary adult naturalisation requirements under section 8 of the Brunei Nationality Act. Birth, indigenous-group, marriage and registration routes are outside this baseline.

facts.label: Twenty years within twenty-five, plus the final two
facts.text: Section 8 requires at least twenty aggregate years of residence during the twenty-five years immediately before application, including residence throughout the final two years. Meeting that calculation does not create an entitlement to a certificate.
facts.locator: Section 8(1)(a)-(b), printed pages 10-11, PDF pages 12-13

constraint.cohort: Ordinary section 8 applicants, also subject to two continuous final years and statutory counting rules

facts.label: Temporary passes are not automatically qualifying residence
facts.text: Unlawful residence and specified custody periods are excluded. Temporary-pass or permit stays also do not count unless His Majesty consents. The Act credits specified absences, including approved education and qualifying government service, so a simple total of entry stamps is insufficient.
facts.locator: Section 8(2)-(3), including the S 29/1995 transfer footnote, printed pages 11-12, PDF pages 13-14

facts.label: Capacity, character, support and permanent intention
facts.text: The applicant must have full capacity, defined as at least eighteen and of sound mind, satisfy the good-character requirement, be unlikely to become a charge on Brunei and declare an intention to settle permanently. These conditions accompany the residence requirement.
facts.locator: Sections 2(2) and 8(1)(c)-(d),(f), printed pages 3 and 10–11

facts.label: Malay knowledge and speaking proficiency are assessed
facts.text: The Language Board must find the prescribed Malay knowledge and proficient speech, with the Act's exception for inability caused by a physical, speech or hearing impediment. The regulations assess practical communication appropriate to the applicant's standing; they do not specify a CEFR level.
facts.locator: Act section 8(1)(e); regulations 9(3), printed pages 4-5

facts.label: The oath and later foreign nationality matter
facts.text: The prescribed oath renounces foreign loyalty and the exercise of rights belonging to another nationality. Separately, voluntary acquisition of another nationality causes loss of Brunei status under section 9(5)(a). This is not a promise that an ordinary naturalised person may freely retain or exercise another nationality.
facts.locator: Sections 8(5), 9(5)(a), 11(3)(b),(4)-(6), and Second Schedule, printed pages 12-16 and 23

facts.label: Form E1, a discretionary decision and the oath
facts.text: The regulations prescribe Form E1 for section 8 applications and Form E2 for the certificate. His Majesty may grant the certificate; the Act requires the allegiance oath and does not turn a completed form into approval. Its section 13 also limits reasons and review of the decision.
facts.locator: Act sections 8(1),(5) and 13; regulations 8 and 16, forms E1/E2/K; current AGC statute register

limits: The current AGC register supplies the 2011 Act and 2002 regulations. Those edition dates are not represented as 2026 enactments. Operational form, interview and documentary requirements must be reconfirmed with Immigration.

The oath is not described here as proof that a foreign authority has already cancelled an earlier nationality. Other countries' retention rules and Brunei's deprivation provisions require separate assessment.

The Act also addresses loss after five continuous years abroad without a substantial connection and an advance certificate procedure under section 9(1)-(3); citizenship should not be treated as an unconditional lifetime status regardless of later circumstances.

topics.title: Brunei Personal Tax Basics
topics.summary: Brunei currently does not levy personal income tax, but that is not a blanket exemption from company taxes, social contributions, financial reporting or another country's tax rules.
topics.scope: Selected individual income-tax scope, the statutory residence definition, employee contributions and cross-border reporting. Corporate calculations, transaction taxes and another jurisdiction's residence determination are excluded.
topics.jurisdiction: Brunei Darussalam: individual tax and reporting

facts.label: No current personal income tax
facts.text: The Ministry of Finance says individuals' employment, self-employment, dividends and interest are not currently taxed, and also identifies capital gains as untaxed. The Income Tax Act's First Schedule limits the income-tax charge to companies rather than imposing it on every individual mentioned in the Act.
facts.locator: MOF FAQ, What type of income is taxable; Act section 1(2), Schedule 1(a)-(b), printed/PDF page 140; S 46/2024 amendments do not replace that Schedule

facts.label: A residence definition is not a personal tax charge
facts.text: The Act defines an individual resident through residence in the preceding year, allowing reasonable temporary absences, and includes physical presence or employment other than company directorship for at least 183 days in that year. That definition does not override the companies-only charging scope or prove residence under a foreign law or treaty.
facts.locator: Section 2, resident in Brunei Darussalam paragraph (a), printed/PDF pages 15-16; Schedule 1; S 46/2024 section 2

facts.label: An incorporated business is a different taxpayer
facts.text: MOF distinguishes untaxed sole proprietorships and business-name partnerships from limited companies. A company receiving or deriving relevant Brunei income is within corporate-tax scope; its owner's no-personal-income-tax position must not be applied to the company's profits.
facts.locator: MOF FAQ, What type of income is taxable in Brunei, opening paragraph and untaxed category 1

facts.label: Covered employees still have pension contributions
facts.text: TAP requires registration and contributions for covered Brunei-citizen and permanent-resident employees below sixty, including several temporary or part-time employment categories. Transitional TAP/SCP arrangements remain relevant for eligible older members who defer SPK conversion; employers must check the member's actual scheme.
facts.locator: Employer responsibilities FAQ, compulsory registration and contributions; Silver Generation and TAP/SCP-to-SPK transition questions

facts.label: No personal tax does not mean no tax-residence reporting
facts.text: Under MOF's CRS guidance, financial institutions collect tax-residence information and self-certifications and report accounts meeting the applicable exchange rules. Brunei does not issue a conventional TIN to individuals; the guidance identifies functional equivalents. A Brunei account or passport does not settle every other country's taxing rights.
facts.locator: AEOI/CRS guidance: wider approach, self-certification, reportable accounts and Brunei TIN information

limits: This is not a statement that all taxes, compulsory contributions or compliance obligations disappear. It also does not establish an individual's entitlement to a treaty residence certificate.

The AGC's 2024 consolidation was read together with S 46/2024, which changes return, assessment and payment machinery. MOF's current FAQ independently confirms the personal-income scope; company rates and filing deadlines are not generalised to individuals.

topics.title: Macao Chinese Nationality Requirements
topics.summary: Macao permanent residence and Chinese nationality are different statuses. An ordinary foreign or stateless permanent resident may apply for Chinese naturalisation, but residence alone does not confer nationality or a Macao SAR passport.
topics.scope: Ordinary foreign or stateless adults applying for Chinese naturalisation through Macao's Identification Services Bureau. Recognition, restoration, descent and nationality choice for historical Chinese-Portuguese cohorts are separate.

facts.label: A Macao passport is not a separate nationality
facts.text: A Macao SAR passport requires Chinese nationality, Macao permanent-resident status and a Macao permanent-resident identity card. A foreign permanent resident does not qualify for that passport merely by obtaining permanent residence.
facts.locator: Travel documents service, target groups and application eligibility; naturalisation service, service target and eligibility

facts.label: Foreign or stateless permanent residents may apply
facts.text: The ordinary local naturalisation procedure is available to foreign or stateless Macao permanent residents. Permanent residence is a prerequisite, not a published automatic nationality grant after a fixed additional number of years; non-permanent residents cannot substitute a temporary work or stay permission.
facts.locator: Law 7/1999 Article 4(1); DSI naturalisation eligibility; nationality FAQ question 3

facts.label: Qualifying grounds and approval are still needed
facts.text: Applicants must be willing to comply with the Constitution and laws and support a qualifying connection or other legitimate reason. DSI identifies close Chinese relatives or reasons such as long residence and connections with China. The director decides applications, with national and Macao security and public order relevant; permanent residence alone does not guarantee approval.
facts.locator: Nationality Law Article 7; Law 7/1999 Articles 4, 9, 10 and 11(2); DSI FAQ questions 4-5

facts.label: Chinese-language knowledge is a listed connection factor
facts.text: DSI lists knowledge of Chinese language and culture among the connections relevant to other legitimate reasons. The reviewed ordinary-route sources do not establish a fixed CEFR level or a universal language-test score; that gap must not be read as a promise that language evidence cannot matter.
facts.locator: DSI FAQ question 4; ordinary naturalisation document list; Law 7/1999 Article 4

facts.label: Renounce foreign nationalities after approval
facts.text: Except for stateless applicants, an approved applicant must renounce all foreign nationalities within six months of notification or the approval becomes invalid. DSI advises against renouncing in advance because refusal could otherwise cause statelessness. Historical nationality-choice arrangements are not a general exemption for new naturalisation.
facts.locator: Law 7/1999 Article 11(3); Nationality Law Articles 3 and 8; naturalisation reminders; DSI FAQ questions 1 and 11

facts.label: DSI examines identity, residence, income and criminal records
facts.text: The service requires the permanent-resident card and supporting identity, nationality, ordinary-residence and financial documents. Overseas criminal records are required for relevant places where the applicant lived at least six months at age sixteen or older. Apply in person through DSI when in Macao; its published procedure allows postal submission from abroad.
facts.locator: Naturalisation service, documents and application location/method; Law 7/1999 Article 4(2)

limits: This summary does not calculate eligibility for Macao permanent residence itself, nor replace DSI's assessment of legitimate reasons. It does not create a separate Macao nationality.
DSI's special guidance about Portuguese travel documents for particular historical Chinese-Portuguese cohorts must not be applied to an ordinary foreign applicant's six-month renunciation obligation.

DSI's naturalisation service was updated on 16 September 2026. The separate nationality law and local application legislation remain the legal sources; personal documents and current administrative instructions need case-specific checking.

topics.title: Macao Personal Tax Basics
topics.summary: Macao has its own tax-residence definition and generally territorial taxation. Work performed in Macao can attract professional tax even if paid abroad; residence does not automatically turn all foreign income into taxable personal income.
topics.scope: Selected natural-person residence, territorial and professional-tax principles under the Macao Tax Code and DSF guidance. Mainland Chinese taxation, corporate passive-income rules and detailed rates are not substituted for individual rules.

facts.label: 183 days or a qualifying habitual home at year-end
facts.text: An individual is resident for the relevant calendar income year after at least 183 continuous or intermittent days in Macao, or with fewer days if a home available on 31 December shows an intention to maintain and occupy it as a habitual residence. A full or partial day counts. Article 24's residence rule took effect on 1 January 2025, ahead of the Code's general 2026 commencement.
facts.locator: Tax Code Article 24(1)(1),(2); approving Law 24/2024 Article 29(1),(3)

facts.label: Territorial scope, subject to specific exceptions
facts.text: The Code generally applies to taxable events in Macao, subject to international or interregional agreements and contrary legal provisions. DSF explains that foreign-source income is generally outside that territorial rule. Its special foreign-passive-income exception concerns qualifying multinational-group entities, not a blanket worldwide charge on every individual resident.
facts.locator: Tax Code Article 14; DSF Article 14 infographic, including its exception for constituent entities under Complementary Income Tax Regulation Article 2(2)

facts.label: Payment abroad does not remove local work income
facts.text: Professional tax covers income from work carried out in Macao, in cash or kind, regardless of where payment originates or is made and regardless of currency. Foreign payroll is therefore not itself an exemption for work performed locally.
facts.locator: DSF Professional Tax introduction, income subject to tax and source/payment-place scope

facts.label: Employees and listed independent professions differ
facts.text: DSF distinguishes employed workers from people independently exercising the listed liberal or technical professions. For employees, its guidance places registration, applicable withholding and periodic remittance duties on employers; it does not classify every independent business as the same professional-tax cohort.
facts.locator: DSF Professional Tax introduction, first and second taxpayer groups and employer obligations

facts.label: Some absent taxpayers need a local tax representative
facts.text: Natural-person taxpayers living outside Macao, and residents absent for more than 183 days in a calendar year, must generally appoint a representative habitually resident in Macao for tax rights and ancillary duties. The Code waives this appointment when the taxpayer opts for the electronic-notification system; this is distinct from the residence test.
facts.locator: Tax Code Article 22(1)-(2), read separately from Article 24

facts.label: Residence evidence and treaty relief are separate steps
facts.text: DSF provides applications for declarations of tax residence and procedures under applicable double-taxation agreements, including mutual agreement requests where taxation is alleged to conflict with an agreement. A Macao identity document alone does not establish that a particular treaty benefit applies.
facts.locator: Tax Code Article 24(3); DSF avoidance-of-double-taxation page, residence declaration and mutual agreement procedure

limits: Macao is assessed as its own tax jurisdiction here. Neither mainland China's individual-income-tax rules nor company-level foreign-passive-income exceptions are copied onto all Macao individuals.

Professional tax is not the entire Macao tax system. Separate business, property, transaction and other obligations can apply; exemptions, source disputes and treaty entitlements require individual analysis.
The Tax Code generally commenced on 1 January 2026, but its residence provision began on 1 January 2025. The two commencement dates must not be conflated.

topics.title: Taiwan Naturalisation Requirements
topics.summary: Ordinary naturalisation requires a qualifying five-year residence history, character and support evidence, and language/civics proof. Nationality permission, loss-of-original-nationality evidence, settlement and household registration are distinct stages.
topics.scope: Selected ordinary adult foreign or stateless naturalisation requirements under Article 3 of Taiwan's Nationality Act. Mainland Chinese, Hong Kong and Macao status routes, descent and exceptional grants are outside this baseline.

facts.label: Five consecutive years with at least 183 days each
facts.text: An ordinary applicant currently domiciled in the territory needs five consecutive years of lawful residence, with at least 183 days in each year. The operative Chinese text includes the 183rd day; it is not a requirement for more than 183 days or a single aggregate across five years.
facts.locator: Nationality Act Article 3(1), opening words and subparagraph 1, operative Chinese text

constraint.cohort: Ordinary Article 3 applicants currently domiciled in the territory, with at least 183 days in each consecutive qualifying year

facts.label: Legal capacity, conduct and stable support also apply
facts.text: The ordinary route requires capacity under both the applicant's national law and Taiwan's law, good conduct without the disqualifying criminal record, and sufficient property, professional skills or other stable means of support. Residence alone does not establish eligibility.
facts.locator: Nationality Act Article 3(1)(2)-(4), with Article 3(2) authorising detailed conduct standards

facts.label: Alternative evidence, not a universal CEFR threshold
facts.text: MOI accepts specified alternatives for basic language and civic knowledge: at least one year at a domestic school, qualifying government courses or the naturalisation test. The ordinary route generally uses at least 200 course hours or a test score of at least 70 out of 100; age and special-route reductions are separate. The test may be oral or written.
facts.locator: Nationality Act Article 3(1)(5),(3); MOI nationality FAQ Q2, evidence alternatives and ordinary-route thresholds

facts.label: Loss of original nationality is usually proved after permission
facts.text: Article 9 generally requires proof of loss of the original nationality within one year of naturalisation permission, or from reaching the age at which the original country's law permits that loss. Verified legal or administrative barriers may justify an extension. Specified high-level professionals, special contributors and qualifying inability not attributable to the applicant have exceptions; retention is not automatic for ordinary applicants.
facts.locator: Nationality Act Article 9(1)-(4), including the cross-references to Articles 5(1)(3) and 6

facts.label: Family and specially approved routes have different rules
facts.text: The Act separately provides reduced or modified requirements for listed family connections and certain specially qualified applicants. Article 5's high-level-professional route requires the prescribed recommendation and review; its shorter residence option is not the ordinary rule for everyone with a job, investment or residence permit.
facts.locator: Nationality Act Articles 4-6, particularly Article 5(1)(3) and (2)

facts.label: Naturalisation is not immediate household registration
facts.text: Nationality applications are decided by the Ministry of the Interior. Newly naturalised people must separately satisfy the applicable immigration residence and settlement requirements; NIA then directs completion of household registration following the settlement certificate. Article 9's restriction while renunciation evidence is outstanding concerns settlement, not a blanket prohibition on holding a residence permission.
facts.locator: Nationality Act Articles 8-9, operative Chinese distinction between residence and settlement; NIA Guidelines 0305 sections II(II), VI(III) and VII(I)

limits: The Chinese Act is used for the inclusive 183-day threshold and the distinction between residence and settlement. Its English translation contains wording that can mislead on those two points.

Naturalisation permission is not presented as an immediate grant of all rights associated with household registration or a passport containing a national ID number. Later immigration and registration conditions require separate checks.

This ordinary-route summary does not establish the applicant's final conduct assessment, recognition of residence periods or entitlement to a renunciation exception. No invented CEFR level is assigned.

topics.title: Taiwan Personal Tax Basics
topics.summary: Taiwan's income-tax residence rules combine domicile and presence, while local-source income and overseas-income basic tax follow different rules. Foreign payment is not enough to make work done in Taiwan foreign-source.
topics.scope: Selected individual residence, local work income, filing and overseas basic-income-tax principles, with the narrowly qualified foreign-special-professional relief identified. This is not a full tax calculation or treaty determination.

facts.label: Domicile with habitual residence, or at least 183 days
facts.text: Article 7 treats an individual as resident if domiciled and habitually resident in the territory, or, without that domicile, present for at least 183 days during the tax year. The second route is inclusive of day 183; citizenship or a residence permit alone does not replace the statutory tests.
facts.locator: Income Tax Act Article 7(2)(1)-(2), operative Chinese text

facts.label: Calendar-year visits are combined
facts.text: MOF's alien-tax instructions use the calendar year and add separate visits together. Arrival day is excluded and departure day is included. The annual tax count should not be substituted for the multi-year immigration or naturalisation residence calculation.
facts.locator: Instructions section I, tax year and calculation of days of residence, points 3-4

facts.label: Local work can be taxable despite overseas payroll
facts.text: Compensation for work performed in Taiwan is generally local-source. Article 8 has a limited exception for a nonresident staying no more than ninety days in the year and paid by an overseas employer. It does not exempt all foreign-paid workers or everyone staying fewer than 183 days.
facts.locator: Income Tax Act Article 8(3); MOF instructions section I.1, distinctions between stays up to 90 days, over 90 but under 183, and at least 183

facts.label: Withholding does not resolve every filing obligation
facts.text: The official instructions distinguish nonresident withholding from declarations for relevant income not fully dealt with at source, including locally earned pay from an overseas employer where taxable. Residents generally make an annual return in May, with departure-related filing rules requiring separate attention.
facts.locator: Instructions section I.1 and I.6, taxpayer categories and time of filing

facts.label: Overseas income can enter the resident basic-tax calculation
facts.text: Resident overseas income is not simply ignored: MOF says qualifying overseas income of at least NT$1 million enters the basic-income calculation. That inclusion alone does not mean extra tax is payable; the comparison with ordinary income tax, applicable deduction and other rules still matter. Any credit for overseas tax is subject to a limit, not an automatic full refund.
facts.locator: MOF FAQs 1744, 1746 paragraph 1 and 1745

facts.label: Foreign-special-professional relief is conditional
facts.text: Qualifying foreign special professionals under Article 22 and its tax-relief regulations can obtain five-year relief starting with their first qualifying year of at least 183 days and professional salary above NT$3 million. The benefit excludes half the salary above that amount from ordinary income and overseas income from basic income, subject to the statutory conditions and an application with supporting evidence; it is not available merely because a worker is foreign.
facts.locator: MOF FAQ 1746 paragraph 2, updated 10 April 2026, referencing amended Article 22 and the foreign-special-professional tax-relief regulations

limits: The English instruction page retains a 2024 heading, but its actual body addresses 2025 returns filed in 2026 and was updated on 27 April 2026. Only its baseline counting, source and filing explanations are used here; its dated rate, exemption and deduction tables are not republished as 2026 amounts.

The overseas basic-income-tax mechanism, local-source tax and special-professional relief are distinct. Treaty relief, household circumstances, foreign-controlled entities and separate property taxes require additional analysis.
The special-professional FAQ summarises a qualified regime, not its complete eligibility checklist. Residence or a work permit alone is not proof that the exemption applies.

review.notes: Independently opened all 26 retained official authorities and checked six topics and 35 facts. Approved after author corrections to Brunei's temporary-permission consent authority and two statutory locators. Actual Chinese Taiwan provisions, Macao Portuguese statutes and DSF infographic, and Brunei PDF editions were read. Explicit gaps, scope, source-edition limits and later residence/settlement distinctions remain integral to approval. See matching review notes for source access and review detail. Publication and deployment are separate.

topics.title: St Vincent: adult citizenship routes
topics.summary: Adult citizenship applications require route-specific eligibility and supporting evidence. The verified seven-year constitutional registration route concerns Commonwealth citizens; the complete ordinary naturalisation rules were not established from an accessible national statute in this collection.
topics.scope: Ordinary adult residence-based citizenship enquiry and the published application process; Commonwealth registration is identified separately, not presented as a universal naturalisation route.

facts.label: Seven years is a scoped registration rule
facts.text: Constitution section 93(2)(b) permits registration of Commonwealth citizens ordinarily resident for seven years immediately before application. Statutory refusal on defence, public-safety or public-order grounds remains possible; this is not the ordinary naturalisation rule for every nationality.
facts.locator: Constitution section 93(2)(b), its proviso and section 94

facts.label: Ordinary naturalisation clock unresolved
facts.text: The Prime Minister's FAQ mentions seven consecutive years of temporary residence or permanent-resident status for registration, without resolving the applicant cohorts. The full ordinary naturalisation clock, qualifying status and absence limits therefore remain unestablished here.
facts.locator: FAQ question 1; Constitution sections 93–94

facts.label: Identity, references and translations
facts.text: The citizenship checklist requests the application and reference page, certified photograph, birth certificate and passport biographical page, with spouse and marriage documents where applicable. Documents not in English require an official translation; originals are returned.
facts.locator: Requirements PDF page 3, Citizenship section and final document note

facts.label: Medical and police evidence
facts.text: The checklist requires the applicant's medical certificate and a police certificate from the country most recently resided in for more than six months before arriving in Saint Vincent and the Grenadines. Additional applicable documents may be requested.
facts.locator: Requirements PDF page 3, Citizenship items iv–v and additional-documents item vi

facts.label: Submission is not approval
facts.text: The office permits submission by mail, courier or a representative without being physically present when filing. Applications require investigation. Remote submission does not establish an exemption from the route's residence requirements or a guaranteed decision date.
facts.locator: FAQ questions 3–4

facts.label: Language and civic standard unresolved
facts.text: The collected official checklist and general guidance do not establish the ordinary route's language standard, testing procedure or exemptions. No CEFR level or exemption from testing is asserted.
facts.locator: Requirements PDF page 3; citizenship guidance, application section

facts.label: Renunciation is a separate enquiry
facts.text: The office describes an application to renounce Vincentian citizenship, supported by the current passport and birth-certificate copy. That procedure does not establish whether an ordinary naturalisation applicant must renounce another nationality or can retain it; those questions remain unresolved here.
facts.locator: Citizenship guidance, Renunciation of Citizenship section

limits: The full current Citizenship Act was not obtained from an accessible national primary source. Constitutional Commonwealth registration and the office's general registration FAQ must not be flattened into a universal naturalisation clock.

The Constitution source is the government's copy marked updated in 2005. The citizenship checklist is undated; conflicting displayed fees are omitted. Descent, marriage and investment routes are outside this collection.

topics.title: St Vincent: personal income-tax scope
topics.summary: Personal tax depends on residence, ordinary residence and income source, not possession of a Vincentian passport. The law has multiple residence tests and a specific receipt-based foreign-income rule for limited resident cohorts.
topics.scope: Baseline individual income-tax residence, income scope and filing; no rates, tax calculation or comprehensive special-regime advice.

facts.label: Residence is not only a day count
facts.text: Residence includes a permanent abode with some presence, at least 183 days in the basis period, or presence continuous with qualifying presence in an adjoining year. The abode test preserves specified whole-year absences for education, medical treatment, government duties or government-sponsored labour schemes, subject to the Comptroller's satisfaction.
facts.locator: Section 2, resident definition (a)(i)–(iii), PDF page 12

facts.label: Resident and nonresident scope
facts.text: Residents generally include domestic and foreign income; nonresidents include Vincentian-source income. Ordinary residence specifically refers to the permanent-abode limb, not every resident. Employment exercised in the country is domestic-source regardless of where payment or the contract occurs.
facts.locator: Section 2, ordinarily resident; sections 8(1) and 10(1)(a)

facts.label: Limited foreign-income receipt rule
facts.text: Residents not ordinarily resident, and ordinarily resident officers or crew of international ships, include foreign income only to the extent received locally. Compulsory remittances under a government-contract overseas labour scheme are specifically included for ordinarily resident workers.
facts.locator: Section 8(2)–(3), PDF page 16

facts.label: Returns and withholding
facts.text: The revenue department lists 31 March after the calendar year as the personal income-tax return and payment deadline. Employer PAYE and withholding on covered payments to nonresidents are separate collection obligations; deductions do not turn citizenship into the tax-residence test.
facts.locator: Taxes page, Personal Income Tax, Pay As You Earn and Withholding Tax sections

facts.label: Agreement-specific double-tax relief
facts.text: Section 60 authorises double-taxation agreements, including source and relief rules, with agreements and changes published by Gazette order. Relief requires checking the applicable agreement; no universal exemption or particular treaty entitlement is established here.
facts.locator: Section 60(1)–(3), PDF page 53

limits: The IRD-hosted statutory compilation is not represented as a newly consolidated 2026 edition. Current guidance was read alongside it; rates, allowances and old subsidiary treaty lists are not reproduced as current entitlements.
General information only. Residence, source, remittance and agreement eligibility require individual analysis; corporate taxation and social contributions are outside this baseline.

topics.title: St Kitts and Nevis: adult naturalisation
topics.summary: Ordinary naturalisation is discretionary and distinct from Commonwealth registration or citizenship by investment. The posted statute requires a final residence year and separately refers to residence during the preceding fourteen years; its unusual wording is preserved rather than converted into a simple total.
topics.scope: Adult alien naturalisation under section 6 and Second Schedule paragraph 1; Commonwealth registration, British-protected-person alternatives, descent, marriage and investment are not interchangeable baseline routes.

facts.label: Final year and preceding-period wording
facts.text: An alien applicant must reside throughout the immediately preceding twelve months. The additional limb says the applicant has resided locally during the fourteen years preceding that year, without specifying an aggregate in that limb. Administrative interpretation of that wording remains unresolved; it is not labelled a simple fourteen-year total.
facts.locator: Second Schedule paragraph 1(a)–(b), printed page 15

facts.label: Absences and excluded residence
facts.text: Absences under six months and approved education, health or prescribed absences can count. Unlawful residence and custody outside a mental hospital do not; temporary immigration permission counts only with ministerial consent. Special circumstances can shift the final twelve-month period back by up to six months.
facts.locator: Section 2(7)–(8); Second Schedule paragraph 2

facts.label: Adult capacity, character and future home
facts.text: The applicant must be at least eighteen, of full capacity, of good character in the Minister's opinion and intend to reside locally after naturalisation.
facts.locator: Sections 2(3), 6; Second Schedule paragraph 1(c)–(d)

facts.label: Discretion, certificate and oath
facts.text: Meeting the qualifications does not compel a grant: the Minister retains discretion. Naturalisation uses Form N1; the oath or affirmation is required, normally within one calendar year of the certificate unless extended.
facts.locator: Section 6; Citizenship Regulations 4–6, printed page 17

facts.label: Language evidence unresolved
facts.text: No named language level, accepted evidence or test exemption was established from the collected ordinary-route provisions. This is not an assertion that no language assessment exists.
facts.locator: Section 6 and Second Schedule

facts.label: Dual-nationality protection is cohort-specific
facts.text: Constitution section 93 protects people entitled to registration under section 92 from refusal or compulsory renunciation solely because of another nationality. That express protection must not be extended to all ordinary naturalisation applicants; this collection does not settle their complete retention conditions.
facts.locator: Constitution sections 92–94, especially 93(1)–(2)

limits: The statutory source is the official 31 December 2020 revision. The separately read September 2026 descendant-registration bill is not treated as an operative ordinary-route amendment.

No single total residence number is asserted from the unusual Second Schedule wording. Commonwealth registration and British-protected-person rules differ. Language and ordinary-route foreign-nationality retention remain unresolved, not waived.

topics.title: St Kitts and Nevis: individual tax scope
topics.summary: The general income-tax charge ceased to apply to individuals in 1980, but this is not a tax-free-passport rule. Unincorporated business tax and withholding on covered payments to nonresidents require separate consideration.
topics.scope: Baseline individual income-tax charge, nonresident withholding and unincorporated business obligations; corporate residence rules are not substituted for personal rules.

facts.label: General individual income-tax charge removed
facts.text: Section 3(3) disapplies the general income-tax charge to income accruing from 1 May 1980 except income of a company liable under that section. The revenue department confirms abolition for individuals; this covers the general charge rather than eliminating every tax affecting a person.
facts.locator: Income Tax Act section 3(3), printed page 11; IRD corporate-income-tax page, opening historical explanation

facts.label: Do not revive old worldwide-income wording
facts.text: Section 3's domestic and foreign-income provisions must be read with the later individual exclusion. They are not a current general worldwide-income or remittance-basis charge on ordinary individuals. Separate business and withholding provisions can still matter.
facts.locator: Income Tax Act section 3(1)–(3), read together

facts.label: Covered payments to nonresidents
facts.text: Resident payers must withhold on covered income paid or credited to nonresidents, including specified interest, rent, fees, royalties and services. Section 36 expressly includes individuals; the payer can have this duty even when not otherwise an income-tax taxpayer.
facts.locator: Income Tax Act section 36(1), (4)–(8), printed pages 36–38

facts.label: Self-employment has a separate business tax
facts.text: Unincorporated business tax applies to covered business carried on locally, including personal services but excluding employment. Its ordinary base uses gross takings subject to statutory reductions, not net salary; qualifying businesses may instead make the Act's continuing election for Income Tax Act calculation.
facts.locator: Unincorporated Business Tax Act sections 2–5, especially 3 and 5(5)–(7)

facts.label: Quarterly business returns
facts.text: Persons liable for unincorporated business tax must file quarterly returns and pay by 15 March, June, September and December for the preceding quarter. Partners are jointly and severally liable, although one partner can be designated to file and pay.
facts.locator: Unincorporated Business Tax Act sections 6–7; section 7 as substituted by Act 6 of 2014

facts.label: Residence and agreement limits
facts.text: No general individual 183-day tax-residence rule was established from these sources. The Income Tax Act allows double-taxation arrangements declared by order to override contrary enactments; any relief must match the relevant person, income and agreement.
facts.locator: Income Tax Act sections 3, 36(5) and 90

limits: The official tax statutes are revised to 31 December 2017. Current IRD confirmation of individual income-tax abolition was separately read. Rates and thresholds, which can be changed or temporarily reduced, are deliberately omitted.
A passport is not proof of tax residence or immunity from another country's tax. Social levies, contributions, VAT, property taxes and special business elections need separate advice.

topics.title: Antigua and Barbuda: adult naturalisation
topics.summary: Ordinary alien naturalisation combines a final residence year with five aggregate years in the preceding seven-year window. Good character, future residence and ministerial discretion remain separate requirements; Commonwealth registration and investment citizenship are different routes.
topics.scope: Adult alien naturalisation under section 6 and Second Schedule paragraph 1, read with the enacted 2021 residence-counting amendment; not descent, marriage, Commonwealth registration or investment citizenship.

facts.label: Final year plus five in the earlier seven
facts.text: The ordinary alien route requires twelve months' residence immediately before application and five aggregate years within the seven years preceding that final year. In special circumstances, the Minister can accept a final twelve-month period ending up to six months earlier.
facts.locator: Second Schedule paragraphs 1(a)–(b) and 2, PDF page 16

facts.label: Permitted absences and amended exclusions
facts.text: Short absences under six months and approved education, health or prescribed absences can count. The 2021 amendment excludes unlawful-residence periods totalling six months or more; it does not establish automatic credit for every shorter unlawful stay. Temporary permission requires ministerial consent to count; custody is excluded except mental-hospital detention.
facts.locator: Act section 2(7)–(8); Act 5 of 2021 section 2 replacing section 2(8)(a)

facts.label: Adult capacity, character and intention
facts.text: Applicants must be at least eighteen and of full capacity, satisfy the Minister as to good character, and intend to reside in Antigua and Barbuda if naturalised.
facts.locator: Sections 2(3), 6; Second Schedule paragraph 1(c)–(d)

facts.label: A discretionary grant and allegiance oath
facts.text: The Minister may grant a certificate after the statutory qualifications are satisfied. Citizenship follows the certificate and required allegiance oath; residence eligibility alone is not approval.
facts.locator: Section 6 and Third Schedule

facts.label: No inferred language exemption
facts.text: The collected naturalisation provisions do not establish a named language level, accepted test evidence or exemptions. Their silence is not a verified exemption from an interview or assessment.
facts.locator: Section 6 and Second Schedule

facts.label: Renunciation and dual-nationality scope
facts.text: Voluntary renunciation has a safeguard against remaining without another nationality. The Constitution's express dual-nationality protection concerns its specified independence-era citizens and registration cohort; ordinary naturalisation retention conditions are not fully established here.
facts.locator: Citizenship Act section 7; Constitution section 115(1)–(2), tied to 1 November 1981

limits: The government's base Act is read with Act 5 of 2021, published 13 May 2021; its older residence-exclusion wording must not be used alone. Commonwealth and British-protected-person routes have different residence rules.

The immigration FAQ could not be independently retrieved beyond search previews and is not cited. Language/testing and complete ordinary-route foreign-nationality retention conditions remain unresolved, not waived.

topics.title: Antigua and Barbuda: individual tax scope
topics.summary: Personal income tax was abolished in 2016, but unincorporated business income, including covered rents, remains a separate tax concern. Its legislation distinguishes employment, local business connections, foreign-source conditions and nonresident collection duties.
topics.scope: Baseline individual employment and unincorporated-business income treatment, incorporated residence definition, foreign-income qualifications and nonresident obligations; not company taxation or a tax calculation.

facts.label: Abolition does not exempt all personal income
facts.text: The IRD confirms personal income-tax abolition followed by unincorporated business tax from 1 July 2016. Self-employment, sole traders, partnerships and covered rents fall within that separate regime; employment income is excluded.
facts.locator: IRD FAQ questions 1–4; Unincorporated Business Tax Act sections 2 and 4(2)(e)

facts.label: Several individual residence tests
facts.text: The business-tax law adopts the Income Tax Act's residence definition: permanent abode plus some presence, at least 183 days in the basis period, or presence continuous with qualifying presence in an adjoining year. The abode limb preserves specified whole-year education, medical or government-duty absences subject to the Commissioner's satisfaction.
facts.locator: Unincorporated Business Tax Act section 2; Income Tax Act section 2, resident definition (a)(i)–(iii), printed pages 6–7

facts.label: Foreign business income is conditional
facts.text: The business-tax charge can cover income arising abroad whether remitted or not. Its foreign-source exemption requires both no incidental connection to activity in Antigua and Barbuda and liability to tax in the source jurisdiction. Separate relief concerns temporary visitors without resident intent and under six months' actual residence in the income year.
facts.locator: Unincorporated Business Tax Act sections 2, 3, 4(2)(d), 4(3) and 10(d)(i); printed pages 7–12

facts.label: Nonresident property and withholding
facts.text: Nonresident rental-property owners must appoint a property-management agent for tax and filing duties. Payments to nonresident individuals can attract withholding for specified rent, interest and other chargeable income; nonresidence is not a blanket exemption.
facts.locator: Unincorporated Business Tax Act sections 16–17; IRD FAQ questions 9–10

facts.label: Returns and agreement-specific exemptions
facts.text: Covered businesses file quarterly and an annual return by 31 March after the year-end. The Act also recognises income exemptions under applicable government agreements; agreement coverage and conditions must be checked rather than assuming automatic foreign-tax relief.
facts.locator: Unincorporated Business Tax Act sections 4(2)(c), 12–13; IRD FAQ question 7

limits: The current official collection uses the 2016 business-tax Act and posted IRD FAQ; the 2019 registration amendment was also read and does not supply a new residence test. The older Income Tax Act is used only for the definition expressly incorporated by the business-tax statute.

No generic territorial-tax or tax-free-passport label is justified. General information only: particular income classification, other-country taxation, treaty access and social contributions require separate analysis. Rates and monetary thresholds are omitted.

topics.title: Panama: ordinary naturalisation
topics.summary: The constitutional ordinary route requires five consecutive years of residence, Spanish and basic civic knowledge. Permanent-resident documentation, financial evidence and an express renunciation are required; naturalisation is not automatic.
topics.scope: Ordinary adult applications under Constitution Article 10(1), excluding the distinct family and birth-nationality reciprocity routes.

facts.label: Ordinary residence route
facts.text: Article 10(1) permits an adult declaration of intent after five consecutive years of residence in Panama. The application sheet requires a permanent-resident card and migration-status certification. This is not five years merely holding any visa; the exact qualifying clock start remains unresolved in this collection.
facts.locator: Constitution Article 10(1); requirements items 4 and 11, PDF pp.1 and 3.

facts.label: Spanish and civic knowledge
facts.text: The ordinary route requires Spanish and basic knowledge of Panama's geography, history and political organisation. The reviewed constitutional wording does not name a CEFR level or establish test exemptions.
facts.locator: Article 10(1).

facts.label: Conduct, means and interview
facts.text: The application requires foreign criminal-history evidence for the relevant origin/residence country, a Panamanian criminal certificate, financial-solvency evidence, a tax-clearance certificate and an interview form. Two listed forms of financial evidence are requested; dependent applicants have additional support documentation.
facts.locator: Requirements items 2–3, 6–8, PDF pp.1–3.

facts.label: Renunciation declaration
facts.text: Applicants must expressly renounce their existing nationality; the application sheet requests an express, irrevocable declaration before a notary. That Panamanian declaration does not by itself establish its legal effect under the other country's nationality law.
facts.locator: Constitution Article 10(1); requirements item 1, sworn declaration, PDF p.1.

facts.label: Naturalised nationality can be lost
facts.text: Article 13 distinguishes birth nationality from naturalised nationality. Express or tacit renunciation suspends citizenship for nationals by birth but causes loss of naturalised nationality. Tacit renunciation includes acquiring another nationality or entering an enemy state's service.
facts.locator: Article 13.

facts.label: Clock and absence detail unresolved
facts.text: The reviewed requirements establish permanent-resident documentation but do not settle which earlier residence periods count or a complete absence-tolerance rule. A numeric permanent-residence or physical-presence requirement is therefore not asserted.
facts.locator: Article 10(1), read with requirements items 4 and 11.

limits: Eligibility to apply is not approval; Constitution Article 12 permits refusal on the grounds it lists.
Article 10(2)'s family route and Article 10(3)'s reciprocity route are separate and are not used to shorten the ordinary baseline.
No CEFR level, test exemption or effect of renunciation under foreign law is inferred. Investor-specific procedures are outside this route.

topics.title: Panama: individual tax scope
topics.summary: Individual income tax focuses on income legally sourced in Panama, not on a passport or where payment arrives. Fiscal residence has alternative presence and permanent-home criteria, and foreign-source classification and treaty relief require separate checks.
topics.scope: Baseline individual income taxation and fiscal residence; excludes companies, multinational substance rules, special zones and investment regimes.

facts.label: Fiscal-residence day test
facts.text: An individual is fiscally resident after more than 183 days, consecutive or intermittent, in Panama in a fiscal year or the immediately preceding year. This tax test is distinct from nationality and immigration documentation.
facts.locator: TAT-RF-013/2024, section VII, printed p.7, quoting Fiscal Code Article 762-N.

facts.label: Alternative permanent-home route
facts.text: A permanent home can establish fiscal residence without satisfying the day test. The tax tribunal explains that the home, economic interests and family interests require substantive assessment: merely owning or renting an available property does not establish residence automatically.
facts.locator: Section VII, printed pp.7–10; Article 762-N, Decree 958/2013 Article 10 and Resolution 201-0354/2016 fifth provision.

facts.label: Domestic-source income
facts.text: Article 694 taxes income produced within Panama irrespective of where it is received and covers national and foreign individuals. Nonresidence is not a blanket exemption: specified services benefiting a Panamanian recipient can be domestic source where they support Panamanian-source income and are deducted by the recipient.
facts.locator: Law 1/2014 Article 3 restoring Fiscal Code Article 694, opening, linked official extract p.1; Law 27/2015 Article 1 replacing paragraph 1(e), linked official extract p.1.

facts.label: Foreign-source reporting is separate
facts.text: DGI's individual-return instructions require entering domestic, foreign and exempt income, then separately remove qualifying foreign-source income when calculating taxable receipts. Foreign payment or a foreign client alone does not determine source; Article 694 and special rules govern the classification.
facts.locator: Individual-return instructions V8, printed pp.2 and 4, income opening and lines 19–21; Fiscal Code Article 694.

facts.label: Residence evidence and treaties
facts.text: A residence-certificate request identifies the treaty or general use and the year concerned. DGI asks individuals for migration movements, identity, housing and other Panama-link evidence. A certificate application is not automatic treaty relief; the applicable convention and facts must be checked.
facts.locator: Questions 3 and 5.

limits: General information, not a personalised tax calculation. Income classification, withholding, filing and treaty conditions require individual assessment.

Article 694's official restoration and the 2015 amendment to paragraph 1(e) are read alongside the currently posted DGI individual-return instructions; this is not represented as a full 2026 consolidated Fiscal Code. The services example is not exhaustive: paragraph 1(e) also has rules for public bodies, non-taxpayers and taxpayers in loss.
The tribunal decision supports residence criteria and evidentiary limits, not a guarantee that another applicant will obtain a certificate.

topics.title: Paraguay: ordinary naturalisation
topics.summary: The ordinary route requires adult status, three years counted from permanent admission, real residence, an occupation or activity and good conduct. An elementary language/civic examination applies, while nationality and citizenship rights have separate constitutional rules.
topics.scope: Ordinary adult nationality by naturalisation before the Supreme Court; honorary grants and birth/descent nationality are excluded.

facts.label: Three years from permanent admission
facts.text: The Court requires three years of residence counted from the resolution granting permanent admission. Acordada 464 calls for continued residence and an actual home in Paraguay; a business address while living abroad is insufficient.
facts.locator: Court requirements: admission card and residence certificate; Acordada 464 Article 42(a)–(b), PDF p.10.

constraint.cohort: Ordinary adult applicant; counted from permanent-admission resolution, with actual continued residence.

facts.label: Absence limitation
facts.text: Article 42(c) excludes the applicant who, despite permanent admission, is absent for periods exceeding three months per year during each of the three years before applying. The source's months are not converted into an invented day count.
facts.locator: Acordada 464 Article 42(c), PDF p.10.

facts.label: Adult status, activity and conduct
facts.text: The Constitution requires adulthood, regular exercise of a profession, trade, science, art or industry in Paraguay, and good conduct. Court guidance requests activity evidence and local and origin-country criminal records; its procedure includes a personal sworn declaration.
facts.locator: Constitution Article 148, printed p.26; Court requirements on profession/activity, records and personal presentation.

facts.label: Elementary language and civic examination
facts.text: The examination assesses elementary knowledge of one official language, national history and geography, and constitutional rules on loss of nationality. It may be oral or written, evaluated by the Court president or a designated representative. No CEFR equivalence or general exemption is established here.
facts.locator: Acordada 464 Article 46, PDF p.11.

facts.label: Multiple nationality and loss
facts.text: Multiple nationality may be admitted through a treaty or constitutional-level reciprocity. Naturalised Paraguayans lose nationality for an unjustified absence exceeding three years declared judicially, or voluntary acquisition of another nationality. These rules do not establish universal permission to retain every prior nationality.
facts.locator: Articles 149–150, printed p.26.

facts.label: Nationality is not immediate citizenship
facts.text: Article 152(2) makes a naturalised national a citizen after two years from obtaining nationality. The Court decides the application; a favourable decision is followed by a fidelity oath and the nationality diploma. Nationality acquisition and political citizenship must not be collapsed.
facts.locator: Constitution Article 152(2), printed p.26; Acordada 464 Article 48, PDF p.11.

limits: The Court's current procedure still expressly invokes Acordada 464/2007; only its relevant nationality provisions are summarised.
The absence rule is preserved in the source's own annual/month wording; treatment of an exceptional absence must be confirmed with the Court.
No guaranteed decision time, foreign-law renunciation consequence, CEFR standard or test exemption is inferred.

topics.title: Paraguay: individual tax scope
topics.summary: Resident individuals' IRP and nonresidents' INR have distinct source rules. Work performed abroad can still fall within the statutory Paraguayan-source definition, and the tax authority's residence guidance must not be replaced by an assumed universal day test.
topics.scope: Baseline IRP/INR treatment for individuals, including foreign residents; excludes corporate IRE calculations and separate dividend-tax rates.

facts.label: Published individual residence criterion
facts.text: DNIT's current INR guidance treats an individual with permanent residence in Paraguay under the migration legislation it cites as fiscally resident. It cites Decree 3181/2019 Article 2. The reviewed guidance does not establish a universal 120-day or 183-day test.
facts.locator: INR question: ¿A quiénes se considera residentes?, individual paragraph and legal references.

facts.label: Resident personal-income categories
facts.text: IRP applies to resident national and foreign individuals and separates personal-service income from capital income and gains, excluding income taxed under IDU. Its baseline is Paraguayan-source income from activities in Paraguay, local assets or rights economically used there, not undifferentiated worldwide income.
facts.locator: Articles 47–49 and 53.

facts.label: Overseas services can be domestic source
facts.text: IRP treats personal services performed abroad by an IRP taxpayer as Paraguayan source when provided to IRE or IRP taxpayers. State-paid personal-service remuneration is also expressly covered. Performing work abroad therefore does not itself establish exemption.
facts.locator: Article 48(2)–(3).

facts.label: Nonresident taxation
facts.text: INR covers nonresidents without permanent domicile in Paraguay receiving covered income. Its source rules include local activities, assets and economically used rights, plus specified services supplied from abroad linked to IRE-taxable income. This is not a general exemption for foreign service providers.
facts.locator: Articles 71–73, especially Article 73(9).

facts.label: Treaty-residence evidence
facts.text: For an individual's fiscal-residence certificate, Resolution 65 requires migration-movement evidence for the requested period and identity documents, with RUC and compliance evidence when the person is a taxpayer. Treaty claims involving another contracting state require its tax authority's residence certificate; residence documentation is not nationality.
facts.locator: Articles 1–3 and 7–9, PDF pp.3–5.

limits: General information, not tax advice. Statutory exclusions, thresholds, withholding, business classification and treaties require separate application.

DNIT's currently posted residence answer still refers to Law 978/1996 and amendments. This collection records that published criterion, not a claim that the old migration statute remains wholly in force or that a permit guarantees foreign treaty residence.
Article 49 has specific overseas public-service and reciprocal diplomatic/consular rules, outside the ordinary private individual scope.

topics.title: Peru: naturalisation and legal transition
topics.summary: Migraciones' January 2026 guidance describes a two-year ordinary residence route. Law 32421 enacted a five-year route but postpones commencement until its regulation is published; this collection does not establish that trigger as completed.
topics.scope: Ordinary adult naturalisation under the currently posted procedure, with the new-law commencement uncertainty explicit; marriage, descent and exceptional routes excluded.

facts.label: Published residence and status conditions
facts.text: The posted Migraciones procedure requires an adult applicant, at least two consecutive years of legal residence before filing, and current resident identity documentation with valid residence. It refers to immigration-status loss and authorised-absence rules; the two years are not a tourist-stay or unconditional physical-presence shortcut.
facts.locator: Opening description and Condiciones, updated 27 January 2026.

facts.label: Means and conduct evidence
facts.text: The procedure requires economic solvency of at least 10 UIT in annual gross income according to migration status; religious applicants have a support-declaration provision. It also requests declarations concerning health, actual address and criminal/judicial/police records, plus Interpol evidence under the stated judicial reinstatement of requirements.
facts.locator: Requisitos and Importante, final judicial-measure paragraph; status-specific documentation.

facts.label: Evaluation requirement
facts.text: Applicants must take the evaluation examination and maintain the necessary conditions during processing. The reviewed current application page does not specify a CEFR level or a complete exemption schedule; neither is inferred.
facts.locator: Condiciones, third bullet.

facts.label: Approval, oath and identity registration
facts.text: If approved, Migraciones arranges the nationality ceremony, oath and delivery of the nationality title. The applicant then uses the title for RENIEC identity registration. Meeting the residence period alone is not an approved nationality grant.
facts.locator: Modalidad: Online, final two paragraphs.

facts.label: Express renunciation rule
facts.text: Constitution Article 53 states that Peruvian nationality is lost only by express renunciation before a Peruvian authority. This does not settle another country's rules on retaining the applicant's existing nationality or invalidate the separate scrutiny of how nationality was acquired.
facts.locator: Article 53, parliamentary edition printed p.38.

facts.label: New law's commencement unresolved
facts.text: Law 32421 Article 17(b) enacts five continuous years immediately before application, but its third final provision starts the law only the day after publication of its regulation. Earlier applications continue under their filing-date rules. The reviewed tracker lists a regulation deadline, not a published regulation; commencement is not established here.
facts.locator: Law 32421 Article 17(b), Gazette p.8; third final, sole transitional and repeal provisions, p.10; parliamentary tracker row 31.

limits: Recheck commencement with Migraciones before acting: an enacted law, a regulation deadline or a draft consultation is not proof that the new route has started.
The two-year description is attributed to the actual 27 January 2026 application guidance, not an unconditional confirmation of eligibility for every September 2026 filing.
The five-year new-law provision is not encoded as a current numeric requirement. Language levels, exemptions and a complete absence-counting rule remain unestablished in this bounded collection.

topics.title: Peru: individual tax residence and income
topics.summary: Tax-domiciled individuals are generally taxed on covered worldwide income; non-domiciled individuals on covered Peruvian-source income. Tax domicile has its own presence, timing and departure rules, separate from nationality and immigration residence.
topics.scope: Baseline individual income-tax domicile, source and double-tax relief; excludes business establishments, special regimes and rate calculations.

facts.label: Worldwide versus domestic-source scope
facts.text: Tax-domiciled individuals are subject to covered income regardless of nationality or source location. Non-domiciled individuals are taxed on covered Peruvian-source income. Holding a passport or receiving money in a particular bank account does not replace this statutory distinction.
facts.locator: Income Tax Law Article 6, PDF p.1.

facts.label: Foreign-individual presence and timing
facts.text: A foreign individual becomes tax-domiciled after more than 183 calendar days of residence or presence in any twelve-month period. Status is generally determined at the start of the tax year, with changes effective the following year. Physical-presence counting includes arrival and departure days, even partial days.
facts.locator: Law Articles 7(b) and 8, PDF pp.1–2; Regulation Article 4(a)(2), PDF p.2.

facts.label: Peruvian nationals and return
facts.text: For Peruvian nationals, Article 7 uses domicile under ordinary law. A Peruvian who lost tax domicile regains it on returning unless the return is temporary, with presence of no more than 183 days in any twelve months; the annual timing rule must also be applied.
facts.locator: Article 7(a), penultimate substantive paragraph, and Article 8, PDF pp.1–2.

facts.label: Losing tax domicile
facts.text: Except for designated overseas public representatives, leaving Peru and acquiring evidenced foreign residence can end domicile when both conditions are met. Without that evidence, the regulation applies loss from 1 January after at least 184 days' absence in the preceding twelve months; departure and return days are excluded from absence counting.
facts.locator: Law Article 7, paragraph following (h), and Article 8; Regulation Article 4(a)(1)–(2), PDF p.2.

facts.label: Limited foreign-tax credit
facts.text: Foreign income tax on foreign-source income taxable in Peru can qualify for a credit capped by both the actual foreign tax and Peru's average-rate limit. Unused amounts cannot be carried to other years or refunded under Article 88(e).
facts.locator: Income Tax Law Article 88(e), PDF p.8.

facts.label: Treaty rules can modify allocation
facts.text: SUNAT explains that applicable double-tax conventions can allocate taxing rights to one state or share them. The relevant in-force agreement and income must be checked; domestic worldwide-income liability does not mean the same income is necessarily taxed twice without relief.
facts.locator: Main explanation under Instrumentos internacionales para evitar la doble imposición, before treaty-directory link.

limits: General information, not a personalised tax calculation; income-category source rules, exemptions, withholding and treaty residence require separate assessment.
SUNAT's annotated law PDFs include historical text boxes. These facts use the operative articles, not the former two-year tax-residence wording.
Fiscal domicile is distinct from the tax-register address and from nationality or the naturalisation residence period.

review.notes: Independently read all 21 official authorities and relevant operative clauses for six topics and 34 facts. Approved after a source URL and locator correction to Panama's 2014 law: the original Gazette endpoint was inaccessible during review, but the linked official Procuraduria extract was actually retrieved and read in full. Verified ordinary-route distinctions, Paraguay's permanent-admission clock and nationality/citizenship separation, Peru's explicitly unresolved new-law commencement, and individual tax residence/source/foreign-income qualifications. Exact-byte approval with source-access details and currentness limits in the matching review-notes. No publication or deployment.
